title: Proud Tek Case Studies — RFID Programs and Deployment Outcomes
summary: How Proud Tek RFID programs actually run in production. Six anonymized case studies covering transit ticketing, hotel-lock retrofits, industrial laundry, brand-protection NFC, library kiosks and event wristbands. We do not publish customer names without explicit permission — the case studies below describe the engineering problem, the chip and form-factor decision, the deployment shape and what the buyer team would do differently next time. Buyers under NDA can request the un-redacted version with named customer references.
heroPoints: Six representative deployments — transit, hospitality, laundry, brand protection, library, events.
Documented chip and form-factor selection, encoding scheme, production volume, lead time.
Honest 'what we would change' section per case study — these are not marketing brochure write-ups.

sections.title: Transit ticketing — multi-million MIFARE Plus program
sections.intro: North American regional transit operator. Annual MIFARE Plus EV1 program for stored-value transit cards across a multi-city bus and tram network. Program has been running for four years on Proud Tek inlays.
bullets: Engineering problem — Replace legacy MIFARE Classic 1K cards with EV1 4K equipment-compatible SKUs without disrupting reader fleet operation.
Chip and form-factor — MIFARE Plus EV1 4K in standard CR-80 PVC card form, single-side full-color art, magnetic-stripe-back for legacy reader fallback during the transition.
Encoding scheme — Per-card AES-128 diversified keys; UID locked; transit application keys delivered to the operator's key management system via SFTP with PGP encryption.
Production shape — Forecast-based safety-stock program with 60-day buffer at our warehouse; weekly call-off shipments under FOB Shenzhen terms.
Compliance — FCC Part 15 certified; conflict-minerals CMRT filed annually; AQL final inspection per shipment with full functional read-test reports.

callout.label: What we would change next time
callout.text: What we would change next time: We over-engineered the initial encoding pipeline with full key escrow. The operator's HSM workflow turned out to be simpler than we planned for. Half the encoding workflow ended up unused. Lesson learned for the year-two refresh: match the operator's actual key management posture, not the theoretical maximum.

sections.title: Hotel-lock retrofit — DESFire EV2 across 4 properties
sections.intro: Boutique resort group with 4 properties across the Caribbean. Migrated from legacy MIFARE Classic key cards to DESFire EV2 across the entire property portfolio in a single coordinated rollout.
bullets: Engineering problem — Aging MIFARE Classic infrastructure with documented sector-trailer attacks in the wild; insurance carrier required cryptographically-secure key cards as a condition of liability coverage.
Chip and form-factor — DESFire EV2 2K in PVC card form, single-side full-color property art, encoded for compatibility with the property's installed VingCard / Saflok / Onity lock mix.
Encoding scheme — Per-property application keys with shared cross-property master key for housekeeping; UID lock; tamper-resistant key delivery via the property management system integrator.
Production shape — Single-shot pilot order of 50,000 cards for staff and engineering testing, followed by 250,000 cards delivered in two staged shipments to align with property opening cycle.
Compliance — CE marked for European travel; functional read-test reports per shipment lot; lock-vendor compatibility validated in-house at our Shenzhen lab before shipment.

callout.label: What we would change next time
callout.text: What we would change next time: We laminated the entire 50,000-unit pilot in matte PVC at the buyer's request, then 60% of properties asked to switch to gloss for the production run. Lesson learned: do a small split pilot lamination test before committing the whole pilot to one finish.

sections.title: Industrial laundry — PPS textile tags, 150+ wash cycles
sections.intro: European commercial laundry service operator handling hospital and hospitality textiles. Required RFID tags surviving high-temperature industrial wash and steam press cycles.
bullets: Engineering problem — Track linen across pickup, wash, finish, fold and delivery cycles. Tags had to survive 95°C industrial wash, alkaline detergent, steam press at 180°C and 150+ cycles minimum without read-rate degradation.

Chip and form-factor — UHF {chip:impinj-monza-r6-p:name} in PPS (polyphenylene sulfide) sealed package, ultrasonic-welded to garment care label. Selected after benchmarking against silicone-encapsulated alternatives — PPS survived hotter cure cycles in the steam press.
Encoding scheme — GS1 SGTIN-96 with operator-issued GS1 Company Prefix; per-tag laser-engraved serial overlay for visual verification under reader-blind conditions.
Production shape — Initial 500,000-tag pilot across multiple linen categories; ramp to 2-million-unit annual run-rate over two years.

Compliance — REACH SVHC declarations filed for PPS substrate and adhesive; CE radio compliance for European deployment; documented 150-cycle survival test report provided as part of the pilot deliverable.

callout.label: What we would change next time
callout.text: What we would change next time: The buyer's first reader fleet was suboptimal for dense-population reads. Half the early read-rate issues turned out to be reader-side, not tag-side. We now recommend buyers run a reader-fleet validation pilot before locking in tag SKUs at multi-million volume.

sections.title: Brand protection — NTAG 424 DNA luxury accessories
sections.intro: European luxury accessories brand. Tap-to-authenticate program embedded in the leather lining of handbags, wallets and small leather goods. Anti-counterfeit + EU Digital Product Passport readiness.
bullets: Engineering problem — Counterfeit production undercutting the brand at 40% of retail price; brand needed a consumer-facing tap-to-authenticate signal plus regulatory readiness for the EU DPP rollout.

Chip and form-factor — {chip:nxp-ntag-424-dna:name} with Secure Unique NFC Message (SUN). 0.3 mm inlay laminated between leather lining and outer hide. Per-tap AES-128 CMAC signature verified by brand-owned backend.
Encoding scheme — Per-tag diversified keys; SUN URL templated to brand's authenticate.example.com endpoint; UID lock; consumer-facing tap counter exposed for analytics.

Production shape — Cut-sheet inlay supply to the brand's existing leather goods factory; brand factory laminated under their own tooling. Volume scaled from 200,000 pilot to 1.5-million-unit annual run.
Compliance — REACH SVHC declarations for the leather-compatible adhesive stack; per-tag UID locking documented; brand-owner key escrow procedure documented for SOC 2 audit purposes.

callout.label: What we would change next time
callout.text: What we would change next time: Initial inlay thickness was 0.3 mm — survived leather lamination but was visible as a faint outline on lighter colors. Year-two switched to 0.1 mm slim-profile inlay; visible-outline reports dropped to zero. Lesson learned: substrate visibility is a real product-design constraint, not just an engineering preference.

sections.title: Library self-service — ISO 15693 book tagging consortium
sections.intro: UK public library consortium covering 12 branch libraries. RFID-enabled self-check-in / check-out and inventory wand support. Tagged collection size approximately 800,000 items.
bullets: Engineering problem — Replace mixed legacy 13.56 MHz tag stock (ISO 14443 and ISO 15693) with a single ISO 15693 standard across the entire consortium for inventory wand interoperability.
Chip and form-factor — {chip:nxp-icode-slix:name} in self-adhesive book label, 50 mm × 50 mm, two-pass installation by library staff (interior dust jacket + reinforcement label over the spine).
Encoding scheme — NISO RP-6-2012 library RFID data profile; primary item identifier in block 0, supplementary fields for owner institution and acquisition date.
Production shape — 800,000-label single-shot order delivered in 8 weekly shipments to support staff installation cadence; pre-encoded blocks aligned with each branch's ILS export.
Compliance — CE marked; FSC-certified paper substrate (library tender required sustainable sourcing); pre-encoding test report per shipment lot.

callout.label: What we would change next time
callout.text: What we would change next time: The consortium's ILS export had inconsistent encoding for older items (acquisition-date field blank for pre-2005 books). 12% of the initial encoding batch had to be re-encoded after the ILS data was cleaned up. Lesson learned: validate the ILS export against the encoding schema before production starts, not after.

sections.title: Event wristbands — UHF cashless payment festival
sections.intro: North American 3-day music festival, 80,000-attendee annual capacity. RFID-enabled cashless payment, access control and zone analytics across the festival grounds.
bullets: Engineering problem — Replace cash-only and credit-card transaction infrastructure with tap-to-pay RFID. Required production lead time aligned to ticket-sales cadence and high read-rate in dense crowds.

Chip and form-factor — UHF {chip:impinj-monza-r6:name} in Tyvek paper wristband for general admission, silicone wristband for VIP and staff. Pre-encoded with EPC SGTIN-96 + back-end ticket-number reference.
Encoding scheme — Per-attendee EPC encoded against the festival's ticketing backend; tap-to-pay routed through merchant POS via festival operator's payment gateway.
Production shape — 90,000-unit pilot 12 weeks before event for staff dry-run; production 80,000 units delivered 4 weeks before event for advance ticket fulfillment.

Compliance — FCC Part 15 certified for the US market; PCI-DSS scope handled by the payment gateway integration (Proud Tek shipped pre-encoded wristbands with EPC only; payment tokens applied at activation by the gateway).

callout.label: What we would change next time
callout.text: What we would change next time: Read-rate at the entry-gate funnels degraded 8-12% when crowd density peaked. Our Monza R6 selection was sound for the price point, but the festival operator's reader placement was sub-optimal. Recommended for year-two: simulate peak-density read-rate at our Shenzhen lab using a body-substitute model before committing the wristband SKU.

faq.question: Why don't you publish customer names?
faq.answer: Most of our buyers operate under supplier-relationship confidentiality agreements that restrict named references in marketing collateral. We respect that by default. Named references are available under NDA to qualified buyers evaluating Proud Tek for a comparable program — request the named-reference list via the contact form.

faq.question: Are the volumes in the case studies accurate?
faq.answer: Volume bands (e.g., '500,000-2 million units annual') are accurate as ranges. Specific commercial details (named operator, exact pricing, exact volume per shipment) are kept under buyer NDA. The chip and form-factor decisions, encoding schemes and compliance scopes described are exactly what we shipped.

faq.question: Can you share the actual test reports for these programs?
faq.answer: Functional read-test reports, AQL inspection records, radio compliance certificates and material declarations from completed programs can be shared (with buyer-identifying information redacted) under NDA. The reports document the test methodology and results — useful for procurement teams evaluating supplier QA process before committing to a pilot.

faq.question: What is your largest single-program annual volume?
faq.answer: Multi-million-unit annual programs (UHF retail source-tagging, transit ticketing, industrial laundry) are part of our standing capacity. We have shipped programs above 5 million units annual; specific largest-program volume disclosed under NDA per buyer's evaluation.

faq.question: Do you have case studies in markets we do not see here?
faq.answer: Yes — these six are representative, not exhaustive. We have shipped into healthcare textile tracking, vehicle ID, livestock ear-tagging, IT asset tracking, anti-counterfeit pharma, supply-chain serialization and more. Mention your industry on the initial inquiry; we will route a relevant case-study briefing for your specific deployment shape.

faq.question: Can we visit a customer site to see one of these deployments in operation?
faq.answer: Site visits to deployed programs depend on the operator's openness to receiving supplier-prospect visits — which is typically low. What we can do is route a peer reference call with one of the buyers under NDA, where you can ask operational questions directly without on-site logistics.
